title: What does the final keyword mean when applied to a class, a method, a variable, and a method parameter?
shortTitle: What does the final keyword mean on a class, method, variable, and parameter?

s1_definition.profdef: The `final` keyword expresses that something cannot change after it is established. On a variable it means the reference or value can be assigned exactly once and never reassigned. On a method it means the method cannot be overridden by a subclass. On a class it means the class cannot be extended at all. On a method parameter it means that parameter cannot be reassigned inside the method body. In every case `final` is a compile-time constraint enforced by the compiler, and it signals intent and enforces immutability of the binding, though not necessarily of the object the binding points to.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, think of `final` as a permanent stamp. A final variable is like Rajesh's account number printed on the passbook — once assigned, it can never be changed. A final method is like the fixed legal procedure for closing an account that no branch is allowed to override with its own version. A final class is like the sealed master rulebook that no branch may subclass or extend. A final parameter is like a form field that, once the clerk writes a value when the transaction starts, cannot be overwritten during that same transaction.
s1_definition.oneliner: `final` means assign-once for variables, no-override for methods, no-extend for classes, and no-reassign for parameters — it locks the binding, not always the object.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The `final` keyword expresses that something cannot change after it is established. On a variable it means the reference or value can be assigned exactly once and never reassigned. On a method it means the method cannot be overridden by a subclass. On a class it means the class cannot be extended at all. On a method parameter it means that parameter cannot be reassigned inside the method body. In every case `final` is a compile-time constraint enforced by the compiler, and it signals intent and enforces immutability of the binding, though not necessarily of the object the binding points to.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, think of `final` as a permanent stamp. A final variable is like Rajesh's account number printed on the passbook — once assigned, it can never be changed. A final method is like the fixed legal procedure for closing an account that no branch is allowed to override with its own version. A final class is like the sealed master rulebook that no branch may subclass or extend. A final parameter is like a form field that, once the clerk writes a value when the transaction starts, cannot be overwritten during that same transaction.

**One line to remember:** `final` means assign-once for variables, no-override for methods, no-extend for classes, and no-reassign for parameters — it locks the binding, not always the object.

sections.s2_technical:
A final variable can be assigned exactly once. A final local variable must be assigned before use and cannot be reassigned. A final instance field must be assigned either at declaration or in every constructor, and then never again, which makes it perfect for immutable fields like an account ID. A final static field is a class-level constant assigned once, typically used for things like the bank name. A crucial point is that final locks the binding, not the contents. A `final List<String>` cannot be pointed at a different list, but you can still add elements to the list it references. To get true immutability you also need the object itself to be immutable.

A final method cannot be overridden in a subclass. This is used when a method's behavior is critical and must not be changed, such as a security check or a fee calculation that regulators require to stay fixed. It also enables certain compiler and JIT optimizations because the method's implementation is known to be fixed. Note that a final method can still be overloaded; final only prevents overriding.

A final class cannot be extended. `String`, `Integer`, and `BigDecimal` are all final, which is part of why they are safe and immutable. Making a class final is a deliberate design choice to prevent subclasses from breaking invariants, especially for immutable value types and for security-sensitive classes.

A final parameter cannot be reassigned inside the method. This does not stop you from mutating the object it points to if that object is mutable; it only stops rebinding the parameter name. A senior nuance is the concept of effectively final: since Java 8, a local variable that is never reassigned is treated as effectively final and can be captured by lambdas and anonymous classes without explicitly writing final. Another nuance is that final fields have special guarantees in the Java Memory Model: once a constructor completes, other threads are guaranteed to see the correctly initialized final fields, which is a cornerstone of safe publication and thread-safe immutable objects.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank requires that an account's identifier can never change once the account is opened, because it anchors every transaction and audit record. This is exactly what a final instance field provides — assigned once in the constructor and never again.

Problem 2 — Regulators mandate that the core fee calculation must be identical across all account subtypes and must never be overridden by a rogue subclass. This is exactly what a final method enforces — subclasses inherit it but cannot change it.

Problem 3 — The bank's `Money` value type must be sealed so no one can subclass it and break its guarantees. This is exactly what a final class provides — it cannot be extended.

Problem 4 — Inside the transfer method, the incoming amount parameter must not be accidentally reassigned mid-logic. This is exactly what a final parameter guards against.

The code has a final `Money` class, an `Account` base class with a final `calculateMonthlyFee` method and a final `accountId` field, a `SavingsAccount` subclass, and a `FinalKeywordDemo` main class that shows each usage with a final parameter in the transfer.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh's savings account SAV2001 with a balance of 1,000,000 rupees, transferring 50000 rupees.

Step 1: The program starts and reads the final static constant BANK_NAME. It is assigned once and used everywhere, guaranteeing the bank name never changes at runtime.

Step 2: A SavingsAccount is created. Its final field accountId is set to SAV2001 in the constructor chain and can never be reassigned, anchoring the account identity.

Step 3: The balance is wrapped in a Money object. Money is a final class, so no subclass can exist to weaken its guarantees, and its amount field is final so it is assigned once.

Step 4: The final method calculateMonthlyFee is called. Because it is final, the SavingsAccount subclass inherited it unchanged and could not override it, so the regulated fee of 100 rupees is guaranteed.

Step 5: The transfer method runs with a final parameter amount. Inside the method the parameter cannot be reassigned, which prevents an accidental logic bug. The balance field, which is not final, is updated to a new Money object representing 950000 rupees.

Step 6: The new balance is logged. Throughout, the final bindings protected identity, the fee rule, and the money type, while still allowing the intended balance change.

```text
INFO: Bank: National Bank of India
INFO: Account SAV2001 monthly fee = Rs.100.00
INFO: SAV2001 transferred Rs.50000, new balance Rs.950000.00
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Create SavingsAccount("SAV2001", Money(1000000.00))
    │
    ├─ final accountId  = "SAV2001"  ──→ locked forever
    ├─ final BANK_NAME  = "National Bank of India" ──→ class constant
    ▼
  calculateMonthlyFee()  (final method)
    │ subclass CANNOT override → returns Rs.100.00 guaranteed
    ▼
  transfer(final Money amount = Rs.50000)
    │ amount cannot be rebound (compile-time guard)
    │ balance (non-final) = balance.minus(amount)
    ▼
  balance: Money(1000000.00) → Money(950000.00)
  (old Money object discarded; new one created — Money is final/immutable)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The final keyword expresses that something cannot change after it is established, and it means a slightly different thing depending on where it is applied, but the common theme is that it locks a binding at compile time.

On a variable, final means it can be assigned exactly once and never reassigned. A final local must be set before use, a final instance field must be set at declaration or in every constructor, and a final static field is a class-level constant. The important subtlety is that final locks the binding, not the contents. A final reference to a list still lets me add elements to that list; to get true immutability I also need the referenced object itself to be immutable.

On a method, final means it cannot be overridden by a subclass. I use this for regulated or security-critical behavior, such as a fee calculation that the regulator requires to stay identical across every account subtype. It also lets the compiler and JIT optimize because the implementation is fixed.

On a class, final means it cannot be extended at all. String, Integer, and BigDecimal are all final, which is part of why they are safe and immutable. I make my value types like Money final so that no subclass can exist to break their invariants.

On a method parameter, final means the parameter name cannot be reassigned inside the method, which prevents accidental logic bugs, though it does not stop mutating a mutable object the parameter points to. Two senior points I always mention are that since Java 8 a local that is never reassigned is effectively final and can be captured by lambdas without writing the keyword, and that final fields have a special guarantee in the Java Memory Model, where once the constructor completes other threads are guaranteed to see the correctly initialized values. That last point is exactly why final fields are the foundation of safe, thread-safe immutable objects in our banking system.

---

keyPoints: final class: cannot be extended (e.g., String, Integer)
final method: cannot be overridden in subclasses
final variable: assigned once, cannot be reassigned
final parameter: cannot be reassigned inside the method body
final reference: the reference is fixed, but the object contents can change
